Finland's warning signs are yellow where most of Europe uses white. Why?
White was already used for speed limits
A white triangle on a white verge is nearly invisible, so Finland and Sweden kept the older yellow.
How many different hoofed animals get a warning sign of their own in Finland?
Four, the fourth being wild boar
Most countries manage with a single deer triangle; Finland is one of the few that separates them.
In the Finnish system, what does a round blue sign tell you?
Shape and colour carry the grammar: round blue commands, round yellow with a red rim forbids, yellow triangle warns.
Which part of Finland has road signs in the Swedish style, lettered only in Swedish?
Åland runs its own road law, so a mainland driver crossing by ferry meets a different alphabet of shapes.
Finland has a warning triangle for a crossroads where nobody has priority. What does it warn of?
That you must give way to the right
That the lights are out of order
That traffic from the left has priority
Most countries leave the give-way-to-the-right rule for the driver to notice; Finland signposts it.
What word is lettered on a Finnish stop sign?
The word stays English across Europe by treaty, so a driver who reads no local language still obeys it.
Two Finnish prohibition signs are blue instead of yellow. Which?
No entry and no through road
Parking rules were given their own colour so that the eye sorts them from the dangers without reading them.
A Finnish roadside sign carrying a figure in megahertz points you to what?
Before a phone could read you the traffic news, the sign was how you found the local broadcast.
At which of Finland's borders is there a sign forbidding you to pass without stopping?
The Russian, Swedish and Norwegian ones
Only the Russian and Norwegian ones
Estonia is the trap: the sea lies between, and Finland has no land border with it at all.
Which of these Finnish signs is a blue order rather than a prohibition?
A minimum limit orders you to keep moving, so it joins the blue family with motorway and one-way signs.
Roughly how long was the Finnish peninkulma before the metric system?
A still older peninkulma of the 1600s was only about six kilometres, so the word nearly doubled in length.
What does the old Finnish counting unit tiu count?
Each trade had its own number: a toltti was twelve planks, a kiihtelys forty pelts, a kerpo thirty-one lampreys.
How many eggs make a tiu?
Twenty was the old shopkeeper's bundle: a puntti of matchboxes counted twenty as well.
What did a Finnish kiihtelys of forty consist of?
Fur was counted and never weighed, and the pelt bundle gave eastern Finland a unit of trade all its own.
The Finnish poronkusema measured roughly what distance?
It was how far a reindeer could pull before it had to stop, and it survives only as a word for very far off.
How far is a kivenheitto in the old Finnish measures?
It was fixed at a hundred kyynärä — a stone's throw turns out to have had a legal length.
How long was the old Finnish kyynärä?
It was exactly two jalka, Finnish feet of about 29.7 centimetres — the foot was the half, not the kyynärä the double.
It is the field one barrel of seed would sow, about 4,936 square metres — a measure of land defined by its contents.
The kappa survives in Finland for selling potatoes. How many litres is it now?
The old kappa held about 5.5 litres and was rounded down when the metric system came, so the sack shrank slightly.
How many naula made one leiviskä?
Twenty leiviskä made a kippunta of about 170 kilograms, so the whole system ran in twenties rather than tens.
In which year did the metric system become compulsory in Finland?
The law passed in 1886 and the system was merely optional from 1887 — the old units were given six years to die.
How long is a kaapelinmitta, a unit still used at sea?
Its odd-looking figure is simply a tenth of a nautical mile, and the nautical mile is a minute of latitude.
At sea a Finnish syli is 1.852 metres. What does it measure?
It is a thousandth of a nautical mile, so soundings in syli turn into miles with no arithmetic at all.
How many sheets of paper make a riisi?
The old counts sat in several bases at once: a tusina was twelve, a krossi 144 — a dozen dozen.
A motti is a unit of firewood. How much is it?
Three and a half cubic metres
Loose goods each kept their own metric unit: the hehto of a hundred litres did the same job for potatoes.
A vakomitta of about 214 metres was the length of what?
The plough set the unit: how far an ox team would walk before it had to be turned around.
Which of these is an official public holiday in Finland?
Christmas Eve is the day most Finns care about most, and it is not an official holiday at all — only a custom.
Between 1973 and 1991, Finnish Epiphany was moved to which day?
Ascension Day was shifted the same way in the same reform, and both were put back when it proved unpopular.
How many days after Easter Sunday does Helatorstai, Ascension Day, fall?
Forty days counting Easter itself, which is why it is always a Thursday however the date of Easter moves.
How many days after Easter Sunday does Helluntaipäivä, Pentecost, fall?
Seven weeks exactly, which is why the Greek name counts to the fiftieth day with Easter included.
Why does Finnish Midsummer Day move from year to year?
It was tied to a Saturday in 1955
It was fixed at 24 June until 1955, when it was loosened onto the Saturday between the 20th and the 26th.
Pyhäinpäivä, All Saints' Day, falls on the Saturday between which two dates?
It too was fixed, at 1 November, until the 1955 reform swept both it and Midsummer onto Saturdays.
Which three Finnish public holidays are also official flag days?
May Day, Midsummer Day and Independence Day
New Year's Day, May Day and Christmas Day
Easter, May Day and Independence Day
Midsummer Day doubles as the Day of the Finnish Flag, which is why the flag is left up through the night.
Which of Finland's public holidays are not Christian in origin?
Independence Day and All Saints' Day
Only two of the fifteen; even Midsummer, for all its bonfires, arrives in the calendar as St John's day.
Which date is Åland's Autonomy Day?
It is a paid day off only for people working in the public sector, so the shops stay open around them.
Why did Saturdays become days off in Finland?
The working week was cut to 40 hours in the late 1960s
Saturday has never been made an official holiday; it simply behaves like one and always has since.
Mikael Agricola's Day on 9 April is also which day?
The Day of the Finnish Language
The Day of Poetry and Summer
Four writers hold four flag days, and each carries a different cause: language, literature, heritage, poetry.
J. V. Snellman's Day on 12 May is also which day?
The Day of the Finnish Language
He argued Finnish into use as a language of government, so his day is about the nation rather than the tongue.
Minna Canth's Day on 19 March is also which day?
She was the first Finnish woman to be given a flag day of her own, and the cause was attached later.
Miina Sillanpää's Day on 1 October is also which day?
She was Finland's first woman government minister, which is why her day is about taking part rather than about her.
What is 6 November called in Finland?
It is also Gustav Adolf's Day, and the Swedish-speaking Finns are the only language group with a flag day.
Which date is the Finnish Defence Forces Flag Day?
Finland keeps three military or wartime flag days: this one, the veterans' day in April and Remembrance Sunday in May.
Who keeps the Finnish name day calendar?
Its Almanac Office holds a centuries-old printing privilege and sends the list to every calendar publisher.
How often is the Finnish name day list renewed?
Names are added and dropped by how common they have become, so the calendar slowly follows the nursery.
Where was the first almanac in Finnish printed, and when?
Helsinki was then a small coastal town; Turku held the university, the diocese and the printing press.
The Finnish name day calendar grew out of which medieval list?
The calendar of saints of the Diocese of Turku
That is why so many Finnish name days still sit exactly where a saint's feast used to be.
Which name day reform added more than two hundred Finnish names at once?
Until then the calendar was almost entirely Swedish and biblical, so the change was a national argument won.
Besides people, which animals have name days in the Finnish almanac?
The dog calendar runs to 659 names, the cat to 593 and the horse to 590 — more names than many human lists.
Finland's Saami name day calendar was compiled in 1997. What has happened to it since?
Nothing — it has never been revised
It is renewed every five years
It was merged into the Finnish list
It holds 566 names and stands exactly as it was written, while the Finnish list has been reworked six times.
A British rump steak and an American sirloin are the same cut. So what is a British sirloin?
The two vocabularies are crossed over, which is how a menu can promise one steak and bring another.
Which cut of beef gives filet mignon, tournedos and the heart of a beef Wellington?
One muscle, three famous dishes: it does almost no work in the living animal, which is why it is so tender.
The British call the tenderloin fillet. What do the Dutch call it?
The Argentinians call the same muscle lomo — every beef-eating country has named it and none agree.
Which cut of beef becomes both corned beef and pastrami?
It is the same forequarter slab that American barbecue smokes for twelve hours — a tough cut three cuisines rescued.
The Argentine cut bife de chorizo is which steak?
It comes out of the short loin, the primal that also yields the T-bone and the porterhouse from the same bone.
The Brazilian picanha is the fat-capped top of which cut?
It is grilled with the cap left on so the melting fat bastes the meat, which is why it is cut as a thick curved slab.
A beef animal carries two skirts. Where are they?
One on the plate, one on the flank
One on the chuck, one on the round
The outside skirt is the better of the two, and both are the cuts that fill a fajita.
Why does shank beef suit a long-simmered soup so well?
Its connective tissue melts into gelatine
The toughness is the point: the collagen that makes it chewy is exactly what thickens the broth.
Besides the strip, which cut does a T-bone steak contain?
The bone between them is a vertebra, so the steak can only be cut from the short loin and nowhere else.
How many primal cuts is a beef carcass divided into?
Round, loin, rib, chuck, plate, brisket and foreshank — lamb manages with four and veal with four.
Which of these is a primal cut of pork?
The pork primals are ham, loin, Boston butt, picnic and belly with the spare ribs — none of the beef words fit.
Hotel rack is a primal cut of which animal?
Veal is divided into just four: legs, loin, hotel rack and square-cut chuck.
Fatback is a primal pork cut in Europe. What is it in North America?
The same piece of the same animal is a named cut on one continent and a leftover on the other.
The French cut hampe is which steak?
It hangs from the diaphragm, which is where the English name comes from and why there is only one per animal.
Which cut of beef is lean, moderately tough and barely marbled?
It needs either moist cooking or very rare cooking: there is no fat in it to forgive a mistake.
What does PCV stand for on a car engine?
Its valve lets blow-by gases out of the crankcase and back into the intake instead of out into the air.
What does EGR stand for on a car?
The valve feeds a little spent exhaust back into the intake, which cools the burn and cuts nitrogen oxides.
A car's fuel vapour canister has a second, more revealing name. What is it?
It is filled with activated charcoal to trap petrol fumes from the tank until the engine can burn them.
In a drum brake, the wheel cylinder goes by which other name?
The master cylinder at the pedal pushes the fluid; the slave at the wheel obeys it, which is where the names come from.
A car's front spoiler has a plainer name that says what it does. What is it?
It dams the air away from under the car; the one at the back is called a wing instead.
A car's prop shaft is better known by which name?
Short for propeller shaft: the same word a ship uses for the bar between engine and screw.
A Panhard rod belongs to which system of a car?
It is the sideways bar that stops a live axle wandering left and right, and it is named after the carmaker.
A pitman arm belongs to which system of a car?
It swings the drag link that turns the wheels, and the name comes from the pit-head machinery it resembles.
What is a car battery's electrolyte made of?
The acid is what makes a leaking battery eat paint and concrete, and why the caps are never meant to be opened.
Which part of a car is also sold as a harmonic balancer?
It sits on the nose of the crankshaft and absorbs the twisting pulses each cylinder sends down it.
An ignition coil is sold under which other name?
A magneto makes its own current and needs no battery, which is why small engines use one and cars do not.
Why does a pipe wrench grip tighter the harder you pull?
Its jaws are serrated and hinged to self-tighten
The hinge lets the jaw bite further in as load rises, which is how it turns a round pipe with no flats at all.
The pipe wrench is widely called a Stillson wrench. Where does that name come from?
The town where it was made
Crescent is the same story: a brand name from the Crescent Tool and Horseshoe Company that swallowed the tool.
A Mole grip is not actually a wrench. What is it?
It locks over centre and stays shut on its own, which a wrench never does and which is the whole point of it.
Why is a twelve-point ring spanner more useful in a tight corner than a six-point one?
It engages the nut at twice as many angles
You only need half the swing to find the next bite, which matters when the wall is an inch away.
A tap wrench turns a tap. What does the tap cut?
A die wrench turns a die, which cuts the outside thread on a bolt — the two tools are a matched pair.
An L-shaped tool made from plain hexagonal wire is called what?
A hex key, or Allen key
There is nothing to it but a bent bar, which is why it costs almost nothing and comes free with flat-pack furniture.
Which wrench has a star-shaped cross-section?
The six lobes spread the load over more metal than a hexagon, so the head is far harder to round off.
What does a torque wrench actually measure?
How much turning force you are applying
A bolt is really a stretched spring, and torque is the only easy way to judge how far you have stretched it.
Which wrench is shaped to grip the nut on the end of a brake pipe?
It is a ring spanner with a slot cut in it, so it can slide over the pipe yet still hold five faces of the nut.
What does a breaker bar give you that a ratchet does not?
A long, hinged handle with nothing inside to break
A ratchet's pawls are its weak point, so the bar leaves them out and takes the whole heave on solid steel.
Bicycle mechanics use a strap wrench, or chain whip, to hold what still?
The sprockets freewheel one way, so you need a second tool holding them before the lockring will budge.
Which wrench does the pipe wrench's job but grips with a chain?
It wraps right round, so it still bites on a pipe too wet, too oily or too large for a jaw to close on.
What has a monkey wrench got that a pipe wrench has not?
Smooth jaws turn a nut without chewing it, which is why Britain nicknamed the serrated kind gas grips instead.
What does a try square actually test?
Whether an edge is at a true right angle
The name is the clue: you try the work against it, and any light under the blade means the angle is out.
In knot language, what does a bend do?
Attaches a rope to an object
The three words are the whole grammar: a bend joins rope to rope, a hitch rope to thing, a loop rope to itself.
A fixed loop at the end of a rope
Securing a load on a trailer
It does not slip and it does not jam, and that combination is why it is the first knot taught at sea.
Which knot is tied to haul a load down onto a trailer?
It builds a loop in the middle of the rope to pull against, so the rope becomes its own pulley.
What is a monkey's fist tied for?
To weight the end of a line thrown ashore
A bare rope cannot be thrown far, so the knot is packed round a weight and lands the line on the quay.
A permanent loop woven into a multi-strand rope
A binding on a rope end
It is not tied but unlaid and rewoven, so it keeps far more of the rope's strength than any knot can.
What does West Country whipping do to a rope?
Keeps its cut end from fraying
A rope's end unlays itself the moment it is cut, so the twine is wound on before the knife comes away.
A taut-line hitch, or midshipman's hitch, gives you what?
A loop you can slide tighter or looser under load
It is the tent guy-line knot: friction holds it where you leave it, and a push with the thumb moves it.
Climbers and cavers use the Italian, or Munter, hitch for what?
Belaying — paying out and braking a rope
The rope brakes against itself through a single carabiner, so a lost belay device need not end the day.
What is a jury mast knot tied for?
Rigging a makeshift mast after the real one goes
It makes three or four loops at once from a single knot, one for each stay the temporary mast needs.
What does a bag knot, or miller's knot, secure?
A load on a pack horse
A miller filled and tied hundreds a day, so the knot had to be made with one hand and shed with a pull.
Which knot makes a carrying handle for a bottle with a narrow neck?
The bottle sling, or jug sling
It closes under the lip of the neck, so the weight hangs on the glass's own shoulder rather than on friction.
Which knot forms the loop of a lasso?
It makes a small hard eye for the rope to run through, so the loop closes smoothly rather than snatching.
A diagonal lashing binds two crossed spars against what?
Racking — the frame twisting out of square
A square lashing holds spars that already meet at right angles; the diagonal one pulls a slack frame back true.
What is a marlinespike hitch tied in order to do?
Turn a bar into a handle for hauling on a rope
Thin line cuts the hands, so the knot borrows a spike as a grip and gives it back when the pull is done.
Which hitch is deliberately insecure, for a job you want to undo in a hurry?
One pull on the free end drops it entirely, which is exactly why it is never trusted with anything that matters.
What makes a surgeon's knot different from an ordinary reef knot?
An extra twist in the first throw
An extra loop at the end
The extra twist holds the first half while both hands let go, which matters when a wound is trying to pull open.
Which knot joins fishing lines of very different thicknesses?
A knot that holds in thick line slips straight through thin line, so joining the two needs a knot of its own.
What makes a ristretto different from an ordinary espresso?
The same grounds, about half the water
Half the grounds, the same water
A lungo is the exact opposite — the same grounds with extra water pulled through them.
How does a lungo differ from an americano, when both are long?
All its water is brewed through the grounds
That is why a lungo is usually the smaller of the two and tastes bitter where the americano tastes thin.
Espresso, steamed milk and a dusting of cocoa
The cocoa goes on the glass before the coffee, so the drink is read from the side as three bands.
Ice cream with espresso poured over it
The name means drowned, and a white affogato adds milk to drown it twice over.
What is in a café bombón?
Espresso and condensed milk, half and half
It is layered in a clear glass on purpose: the milk is denser, so the two refuse to mix until you stir.
What is in a café miel?
Espresso, steamed milk, cinnamon and honey
Miel is honey; a melya swaps the milk for cocoa powder and keeps the honey.
Roughly what is a mocha, by proportion?
A third espresso, two thirds milk, plus chocolate
Espresso with cocoa dusted on top
It is a latte with the chocolate added, which is why it arrives in a latte glass and not a small cup.
What is an espresso romano served with?
A sugar cube on a spoon
The acid sharpens a dark roast; a guillermo goes further and pours the espresso straight over lime.
An espresso drawn with cold water instead of hot
A double espresso in a tall glass
Cold water pulls far less of the bitter compounds, so the shot tastes sweeter and takes much longer.
A red eye is brewed coffee with one espresso shot. What is a dead eye?
Espresso with no water at all
Two shots make a black eye, so the row runs red, black, dead — darker names for stronger coffee.
In Turkish coffee, what does orta şekerli mean?
The sugar goes in before the brewing and cannot be changed after, so you order the sweetness with the coffee.
What is in a Cuban cortadito?
Café cubano with a splash of milk
Café cubano itself is espresso brewed with the sugar already in the basket, which is what whips up its foam.
What is mixed with the coffee in Indian filter coffee?
Chicory, a fifth to a third of the blend
Chicory root is roasted and ground like coffee; it was once a wartime stretch and is now part of the taste.
What is a Mexican café de olla brewed in, and with what?
A clay pot, with cinnamon and piloncillo sugar
An iron pot, with orange peel
The unglazed clay is said to be half the flavour, which is why the pot is never scrubbed clean.
What is a double double in Canada?
Drip coffee with two creams and two sugars
Two espresso shots in one cup
A double espresso with two sugars
A whole country orders coffee in a code that nobody outside it can decipher at the counter.
What is a Greek frappé whipped up from?
Instant coffee, sugar and milk or water
Filter coffee blended with ice cream
It is the one drink where instant coffee is the right answer: only spray-dried granules give that stiff foam.
Two espresso shots shaken with sugar and ice
Shaking rather than stirring is the point: the air whipped in is what gives it the thick collar of foam.
A manilo is one espresso shot with under 100 ml of steamed milk. What is it close to?
The whole difference between the milk drinks is the ratio, and 100 ml is where the flat white sits.
Roughly how hot is the water that is forced through espresso grounds?
Boiling water scalds the grounds and turns the shot bitter, which is why the machine holds just below it.
What is the pale foam on top of a good espresso called?
It is emulsified coffee oil and dissolved gas, and it collapses within a minute — which is why espresso is drunk at once.
What makes a chai latte a dirty chai latte?
A plain chai latte has no coffee in it at all, so the espresso is the only thing that makes it a coffee drink.
What is yuenyeung, from Hong Kong?
The name means mandarin ducks, which are always seen as a pair — two drinks that go together.
What is a black tie, in coffee terms?
Thai iced tea with a double espresso
A single shot makes it a red tie, so the strength is worn as a change of neckwear.
What is dalgona coffee made by doing?
Whipping instant coffee and sugar into a foam
It is the Indian beaten coffee by another name, and it needs instant coffee because ground coffee will not whip.
Halloumi holds protected status as the cheese of which country?
The protected name covers all three of its spellings at once: Χαλλούμι, Halloumi and the Turkish Hellim.
Feta is protected as a cheese of Greece. What is Bulgaria's equivalent called?
Because Greece holds the name, every other country's white brined cheese has to be sold under its own.
Oscypek is a protected cheese of which country?
Slovakia's near-identical smoked sheep cheese had to be registered separately, as oštiepok.
Havarti, Danbo, Esrom and Danablu are the protected cheeses of which country?
Four of them, where Sweden managed to register only one cheese on the whole European list.
Svecia is the only protected cheese of which country?
Finland has none at all on the European list, so neither Finnish nor Norwegian cheese appears on it.
Tiroler Bergkäse and Gailtaler Almkäse come from which country?
Germany has the closest rival in Allgäuer Bergkäse — mountain cheeses from either side of the same range.
Fromage de Herve is the one protected cheese of which country?
Belgium has one and France has more than fifty, which gives some idea of how the list is weighted.
Imokilly Regato is the protected cheese of which country?
The name sounds Italian and the cheese is Irish, which is exactly the confusion the protected list exists to settle.
Caerphilly is the traditional cheese of which part of the United Kingdom?
Dunlop belongs to Ayrshire in Scotland and Wensleydale to Yorkshire, each registered to its own valley.
Both White Stilton and Blue Stilton are protected. Which country are they from?
Two cheeses, one name and one protected registration covering the pair — which is unusual on the list.
Queijo Serra da Estrela and Queijo S. Jorge come from which country?
Every Portuguese entry begins with queijo, the word for cheese, so the list reads as a sentence.
Boerenkaas and Boeren-Leidse met sleutels are protected cheeses of which country?
Boeren means farmer: the protection is on cheese made on the farm from the farm's own raw milk.
Which common spice is a dried flower bud?
The bud is picked before it opens; if the tree is allowed to flower, there is no clove left to harvest.
Which part of the saffron crocus is the spice itself?
Each flower carries three, picked by hand, which is the whole reason for the price rather than any rarity of the plant.
Mace comes from which part of the nutmeg?
The lacy coat around the seed
One fruit gives two spices: the seed is nutmeg and the net around it, dried flat, is mace.
Turmeric and ginger are both which part of their plant?
The rhizome, a swollen underground stem
Galangal and fingerroot are the same thing from the same family, which is why they all look like knuckles.
Cumin, coriander, dill, caraway, fennel and anise all belong to which plant family?
They all make the same umbrella of tiny flowers, and the spice is the dried fruit of it every time.
Basil, oregano, thyme, rosemary, sage and mint all belong to which family?
They share a square stem and paired leaves, and the spice is a leaf in every case — never a seed.
Star anise is which part of its plant?
It is no relation of anise at all: anise is in the carrot family and star anise in a family of its own.
Juniper berries are not berries. What are they?
Juniper is a conifer, so the fleshy cone is the nearest thing to a berry the plant can make.
Allspice is which part of its plant, and what family is that plant in?
The unripe fruit of a myrtle
The flower bud of a myrtle
The seed of a pepper vine
It is the clove tree's relative, which is how one fruit came to taste of cloves, nutmeg and cinnamon at once.
Dried latex from a root or rhizome
The plant is a giant relative of fennel, so the most pungent spice in the shop comes from the carrot family.
Mastic, used in Greek and Turkish sweets, is what kind of material?
The tree is a pistachio relative, and the resin is still collected by scoring the trunk and letting it weep.
Wasabi is which part of the plant, and what family is it in?
The rhizome, in the cabbage family
The root, in the pepper family
The leaf, in the mint family
The seed, in the mustard family
Horseradish and mustard are in the same family, which is why all three burn in the nose rather than on the tongue.
Annatto, the colouring in many cheeses, comes from what?
The seeds of a tropical tree
The bark of a tropical tree
The seed coat gives a strong orange with almost no flavour, which is exactly what a cheesemaker wants.
Which part of the liquorice plant carries the flavour?
Liquorice is a legume, so the plant is a cousin of the pea and the bean rather than of any spice tree.
Capers are which part of their plant?
If the bud is left on the bush it becomes a caperberry, which is sold as a different pickle entirely.
Which of these is not a true pepper, botanically speaking?
Chilli is a nightshade, closer kin to the tomato and the potato than to anything in the pepper family.
Sichuan pepper belongs to which plant family?
The curry leaf is a citrus relative too, which is why both smell faintly of peel when crushed.
Bay leaves come from a tree in which family?
Cinnamon and cassia are laurels as well, so the spice rack holds three parts of one family tree.
Besides its bark, what else is harvested from the cassia tree as a spice?
Cassia buds look like cloves and taste like cinnamon, which is a fair summary of the whole laurel family.
Fenugreek, liquorice, carob and rooibos all belong to which family?
Four flavours that taste nothing alike, all from plants that fix nitrogen in little nodules on their roots.
Sumac, the sour red spice of Middle Eastern cooking, is which part of the plant?
It is in the cashew and mastic family, so the spice rack's sour note and its chewing resin are cousins.
Chicory, long used to stretch coffee, is which part of the plant?
It is a daisy relative with a blue flower, and the root roasts dark enough to pass for coffee in a shortage.
Coffee and quinine come from plants in the same family. Which part gives quinine?
Coffee is the seed of its fruit and quinine the bark of its tree, from two branches of the madder family.
The Hungarian forint is unusual among currencies. Why?
It has no fractional unit in use
Its subunit is a coin only
The fillér was abolished when inflation made it worthless, so Hungary prices everything in whole forints.
What is the hundredth part of a Czech koruna called?
The word is German for a small coin, and it travelled across central Europe faster than the currencies did.
What is the hundredth part of an Icelandic króna called?
Three Nordic currencies spell nearly the same word three ways: eyrir, øre and öre.
What is the hundredth part of a Swiss franc called?
Switzerland has four languages, so the same coin is a rappen, a centime, a centesimo and a rap depending on where you stand.
What is the hundredth part of a Polish złoty called?
Złoty means golden, so the currency is literally a golden coin broken into a hundred small ones.
Which three countries' currencies are divided into kopecks?
Ukraine's currency is the hryvnia and Belarus's the ruble, yet all three kept the same word for the small change.
What is the hundredth part of a Turkish lira called?
The para was the older subunit and still survives in Serbia, where a dinar is divided into a hundred of them.
The leu is the currency of Romania and of which other country?
Bulgaria's lev, Albania's lek and Macedonia's denar all sound close and are four separate currencies.
Which of these is the currency of Kazakhstan?
Kazakhstan shares the telephone code +7 with Russia, but it has had its own money since 1993.
Which currency is divided into satang?
Four neighbours, four currencies and four different names for the small change — kip, riel, kyat and baht.
What is the currency of Mongolia?
Its hundredth part is the möngö, which is also the Mongolian word for silver.
Which currency is divided into agorot?
Its neighbours divide their money into fils and piastres, words that came with the Ottoman administration.
What is the currency of Botswana?
Pula means rain in Setswana, which in a country largely desert is the same thing as saying wealth.
Which currency is divided into pesewas?
Nigeria's naira divides into kobo and Gambia's dalasi into bututs, so no two neighbours agree.
What is the currency of Ethiopia?
Eritrea, which separated from it, chose the nakfa instead — named after the town its independence war was run from.
What is the currency of Madagascar?
Its subunit is the iraimbilanja, and the ariary is one of very few currencies not divided into hundredths.
What is the currency of Guatemala?
It is named after the bird on the flag, which Mayan rulers valued for its tail feathers rather than its meat.
Which Central American currency is named after an indigenous chief who resisted the Spanish?
The colón and the balboa are named after the Europeans instead — Columbus and Balboa.
What is the currency of Haiti?
The name comes from the gourd, which an early ruler is said to have made legal tender to steady the economy.
Which country's currency is the dalasi?
Four African countries beginning with G and four completely different currencies: dalasi, cedi, franc and CFA franc.
Finland's dialling code is +358. Which country is +385?
The two look almost alike on a screen, and a mistyped digit sends the call to the Adriatic.
Which three Baltic states have the codes +370, +371 and +372, in that order?
The codes run south to north, which is the opposite of the order most people recite the three countries in.
Which two countries share the dialling code +7?
Zone 7 was the Soviet Union's, and Kazakhstan has simply never moved out of it.
Canada and the United States share +1. What else is in that numbering plan?
Jamaica, Barbados and a dozen more dial as if they were American area codes, which is why +1 876 reaches Jamaica.
Greenland is +299 and the Faroe Islands +298. Which zone is that?
Zone 2 filled up with leftovers, so Aruba and the British Indian Ocean Territory ended up in Africa's block too.
Japan is +81 and South Korea +82. Which country holds +86?
Taiwan is +886 and Hong Kong +852: a third digit marks whoever arrived at the numbering plan late.
Bangladesh is +880 and Sri Lanka +94, so the subcontinent's codes are not in any geographic order.
Only two African countries have a two-digit dialling code. Which two?
Two digits went to the places telephoned earliest and most; every other African country needs three.
The Pitcairn Islands dial through +64 as well, which makes them the remotest place on New Zealand's exchange.
Argentina is +54 and Chile +56, so the single-digit second column runs roughly from north to south.
What is the code +800 reserved for?
There is a code for almost everything: +888 is kept for disaster relief and +870 for ships at sea.
Vatican City has the code +379. What does it actually use?
The code was assigned and never brought into use, so a Vatican number is in practice a Rome number.
Turkey is +90. Which code does Northern Cyprus dial through?
The telephone system follows the politics exactly: the island's two halves are dialled as two different countries.
At about what age does a Finnish child start the nine-year peruskoulu?
A free preschool year at six has been offered since 1996, and almost every family takes it even though it is voluntary.
Which grades make up the alakoulu, the lower stage of Finnish comprehensive school?
The yläkoulu takes grades 7 to 9, and the division is the only break in nine unstreamed years.
What is the grading scale in a Finnish comprehensive school?
The scale starts at four because four is the fail: the numbers below it would have nothing left to mean.
A Finnish pupil who ends the spring with a grade of four must do what?
Sit a separate exam at the end of the summer
Take the subject again next year
The summer exam is a second chance built into the system, so a single failed subject does not cost a year.
What is the top grade in the Finnish matriculation examination?
The grades are set by percentile, so the number of laudaturs each year is decided before the papers are read.
What is a kaksoistutkinto in Finland?
A vocational qualification plus the matriculation exam
There is even a kolmoistutkinto, which adds a third certificate on top of the two.
Which Finnish institutions may award a doctorate?
A university of applied sciences can award a master's degree, but the licentiate and the doctorate stay with the universities.
Since when has Finland had free universal daycare?
The right came before the preschool year did, so the youngest children were served first by a decade.
How long does a bachelor's degree take at a Finnish university of applied sciences?
Three and a half to four and a half years
It runs slightly longer than a university bachelor's because a work placement is built into it.
A Finnish bachelor may enter a master's at a university of applied sciences only after what?
The degree is designed around working life, so the work has to come before the study rather than after it.
A Finnish road outside a built-up area carries no speed sign. What is the limit?
The 50 of a built-up area and the 80 outside it are the two defaults every other sign is an exception to.
What is the speed limit on a Finnish pihakatu, a yard street?
It is the lowest limit on any Finnish road — lower even than the 30 of an ordinary residential street.
Finnish motorways run at 120 km/h in summer. What happens in winter?
Motorways near towns are kept at 100 all year round, so the seasonal change only shows out in the country.
What is the top speed for a moped in Finland?
A snowmobile may do 60 on land and 80 on ice, which makes it the faster machine of the two.
A snowmobile may do 60 km/h on land in Finland. What may it do on ice?
Ice is the smoother surface, so the limit goes up rather than down — the opposite of what most people guess.
What is the limit for a Finnish car towing a heavy trailer?
A light trailer allows 100, and towing a broken-down vehicle drops you all the way to 60.
Below what height must a child use a safety seat in a Finnish car?
The law says 135, but the Road Safety Council recommends a booster until 150 — where the belt crosses the shoulder properly.
Why should a Finnish driver switch headlights on by hand rather than leave them on Auto?
Automatic mode may leave the tail lights off
Daytime running lights at the front only mean a car is invisible from behind in sleet, which is exactly when it matters.
What does a bar under a laundry symbol mean?
Treat it more gently than usual
Two bars mean very gentle, and a cross through the symbol is the only thing that forbids it outright.
On a care label, what does the triangle stand for?
Four shapes carry the whole code: a tub washes, a triangle bleaches, a square dries and a circle is professional.
Two diagonal lines inside the bleaching triangle mean what?
An empty triangle allows either kind, so the lines are a restriction rather than a permission.
What does a circle inside a square mean on a care label?
A circle on its own is the dry cleaner's symbol; put it in a square and it becomes a machine with a drum.
What does the letter P inside a circle tell a dry cleaner?
An F in the circle means hydrocarbon solvent only, so one letter decides which machine the garment goes into.
What does the letter W inside a circle mean?
It is cleaning with water done by a professional machine, which is a different trade from dry cleaning altogether.
What does one dot inside the iron mean?
Three dots is the hottest at about 200 °C, so each dot is worth roughly forty-five degrees.
What does a hand inside the washtub mean?
The temperature comes with the symbol: a hand means forty degrees even when no number is printed.
How many bars under the washtub means the gentlest wash?
No bar is a full cotton wash, one bar is synthetics and two bars is wool or silk — the bars count down the agitation.
In the American care system, what replaces the number in the washtub?
One dot is 30 °C and four dots 60 °C, so the same dot means temperature in a tub and in an iron but on two scales.
A care label gives the harshest treatment allowed. What may you always do instead?
The label is a ceiling and never a floor, which is why a thirty-degree wash is safe on a forty-degree label.
GINETEX, which created the care symbols, was founded in which year?
The symbols were invented so that a label could cross a border without being reprinted in another language.
Halving an A4 sheet gives an A5 of exactly the same proportions. Which ratio does that?
One to the square root of two
One to one and a half
It is the only ratio that survives being halved, which is the whole reason the A series was invented.
What is the area of a sheet of A0?
Every other A size is a halving of it, so A4 is one sixteenth of a square metre and its weight follows from that.
Roughly what does one A4 sheet of 80-gram paper weigh?
Because A0 is a square metre, the sum is easy: 80 grams divided by sixteen, which is why postage is reckoned in sheets.
What is the C series of paper sizes for?
Each C size falls between the matching A and B sizes, which is exactly the slack an envelope needs to swallow a letter.
Which envelope takes an A4 letter without folding it?
A C5 takes the same letter folded once and a C6 folded twice, so the three cover a whole filing habit.
Where does a B paper size fall in relation to the A sizes?
Its area is the geometric mean of the two, which is why B5 is the usual size for a book and A5 feels small.
What are the dimensions of US Letter paper?
It is 8.5 by 11 inches, so it is wider and shorter than A4 — which is why printing one on the other always clips something.
Ledger paper is which size turned sideways?
Eleven by seventeen inches either way: the name changes with the orientation and nothing else does.
Who first noticed the advantage of a square-root-of-two paper shape, in 1786?
He wrote it in a letter; Porstmann turned it into a system and Germany published it as DIN 476 in 1922.
In which year did the A series become ISO 216 and the United Nations' document format?
Germany had used it since 1922, so the world took half a century to adopt a standard that was already finished.
Japan has its own B series. How does it differ from the ISO one?
Its area is 1.5 times the matching A size
Its area is twice the A size
China went the other way and adopted the ISO A and B series, then added a D series of its own.
How long is a barleycorn, the step between British shoe sizes?
It is a grain of barley laid end to end, and three of them made the inch before the inch was defined any other way.
One Paris point, the step in Continental shoe sizes, is how long?
Six and two thirds of a millimetre: a step small enough that one size up is barely seven millimetres of toe room.
What does a Continental shoe size actually measure?
The length of the last, not the foot
The length of the foot in centimetres
The last is two to two and a half Paris points longer than the foot, which is the room your toes live in.
A US men's shoe size is usually what, compared with the British size?
US men's 13 is British 12, so the two scales count the same barleycorns from different starting points.
What two measurements does a Mondopoint shoe size give?
Foot length and width in millimetres
A label reading 280/110 is a 280-millimetre foot 110 millimetres across, which is why armies use the system.
Which organisation sizes its footwear in Mondopoint?
Japan, China, Korea and the old Soviet Union adopted it as well, so most of the world's boots are measured in millimetres.
What is the step between Mondopoint sizes for ordinary footwear?
Protective footwear steps by 7.5 mm instead, because a work boot does not need to fit as closely.
A child's British shoe size zero is how long?
From there the scale climbs in thirds of an inch to 13½, and then adult size 1 starts the count again.
Brazil uses the Paris point system with one change. What is it?
It subtracts two from the result
So a Brazilian 38 is a European 40, which catches out anyone who buys shoes on holiday there.
A metric tablespoon is 15 ml almost everywhere. Where is it 20 ml?
An Australian recipe written in tablespoons gives a third more than the same recipe read anywhere else.
How big is a metric cup?
The American cup is about 237 ml, so a cake baked from a US recipe in metric cups gets five per cent too much of everything.
Which is bigger, a British pint or an American one?
The British, by about a fifth
The American, by about a fifth
The American, by about a tenth
A British pint is twenty fluid ounces and an American one sixteen, and the ounces themselves differ too.
A dash is an eighth of a teaspoon. What is a pinch?
The whole ladder halves: a saltspoon a quarter, a dash an eighth, a pinch a sixteenth and a smidgen a thirty-second.
What fraction of a teaspoon is a smidgen?
A drop is smaller still at one ninety-sixth, which is as finely as the old kitchen ever bothered to divide anything.
Why is flour better weighed than measured by the cup?
Packing can change the amount by about a fifth
It absorbs water from the air
Scales are more precise for everything
Flour's density is about 0.7 grams per millilitre loose, so how hard you pressed the cup is part of the recipe.
Which of these is the densest in a kitchen, by volume?
Salt is about 1.2 grams per millilitre, butter 0.9, sugar 0.8 and flour 0.7 — a spoonful of each weighs something different.
In older European recipes, what does a pound usually mean?
The Dutch ons in the same recipes means 100 grams, so both old words were quietly rounded to metric numbers.
How many millilitres is an imperial fluid ounce?
The American fluid ounce is about 29.6 ml, so the American ounce is the larger one even though the American pint is smaller.
What was a British breakfast cup in old recipes?
A tumbler was ten and the plain cup six, so a Victorian recipe measured by which crockery you reached for.
What is a dessertspoon standardised at in Australia?
It sits exactly between the teaspoon and the tablespoon, which is why it vanished from most modern recipe books.
What does e.g. stand for in Latin?
It means for the sake of an example, so i.e. — id est, that is — introduces the only item and e.g. one of several.
What does viz. stand for, and what does it mean?
Vice versa — the other way round
The z is not a z at all: it is a medieval shorthand squiggle for the ending -et, misread as a letter ever since.
What does cf. ask a reader to do?
It is short for confer, and it marks a comparison rather than the plain look-this-up of q.v.
What does ibid. mean in a footnote?
In the same place as the note just before
In the work cited much earlier
Op. cit. is the one that means in the work already cited, which may be twenty pages back.
What does sic in square brackets tell you?
The mistake was in the original
It is short for sic erat scriptum, thus it was written: the quoter is clearing themselves of the blame.
Which was to be demonstrated: it does not mean proved but rather that the thing promised at the start has arrived.
What does P.S. stand for, and what comes after a second one?
Post post scriptum means after after the writing, which is as redundant in Latin as it sounds in English.
Meridiem is noon, so noon itself is neither a.m. nor p.m. and twelve o'clock is strictly speaking unlabelled.
What does the abbreviation lb for pound come from?
Libra was a Roman unit of weight, which is why the symbol has an l and a b and the word has neither.
What does stat. mean on a prescription?
It is short for statim; p.r.n. is pro re nata, as needed, and q.d. is quaque die, every day.
What does nem. con. mean after a vote?
Nemine contradicente leaves room for abstentions, which is why it is not the same as unanimous.
What does fl. before a date mean?
The years the person is known to have been active
The year they came to the throne
Floruit means flourished, and it is used when nobody knows when the person was born or when they died.
Inter alia is the one that means among other things, and the two are confused constantly in print.
What does N.N. stand for when a name is unknown?
It means I do not know the name, and it is still printed on concert programmes when a soloist is unconfirmed.
What does s.v. mean in a reference to a dictionary?
Sub verbo, under the word: it points at an alphabetical place rather than a page, so it survives new editions.
What does v.i. mean in a text?
Vide infra, see below; v.s. is vide supra, see above — two letters that send a reader in opposite directions.
What does curriculum vitae literally mean?
Curriculum is a running track, so the document is literally the lap you have run so far.
A way of working: the phrase came out of Latin grammar into police work and then into everyday speech.
